source_text: Τὰ δὲ περὶ τῆς εἰδωλολατρείας ὡς ἴδια τῶν ἀπὸ τοῦ λόγου ἐκτιθέμενος καὶ ὑποκατασκευάζει λέγων αὐτοὺς διὰ τοῦτο μὴ νομίζειν αὐτοὺς χειροποιήτους θεοὺς, ἐπεὶ μὴ εὔλογόν ἐστι τὰ ὑπὸ φαυλοτάτων δημιουργῶν καὶ μοχθηρῶν τὸ ἦθος εἰργασμένα εἶναι θεοὺς, πολλάκις καὶ ὑπὸ ἀδίκων ἀνθρώπων κατασκευασθέντα. ἐν τοῖς ἑξῆς οὖν θέλων αὐτὸ κοινοποιῆσαι ὡς οὐ πρῶτον ὑπὸ τούτου εὑρεθὲν ἐκτίθεται Ἡρακλείτου λέξιν τὴν λέγουσαν· „ὅμοια, ὡς εἴ τις τοῖς δόμοις λεσχηνεύοιτο, ποιεῖν τοὺς προσιόντας ὡς θεοῖς τοῖς ἀψύχοις.“ οὐκοῦν καὶ περὶ τούτου λεκτέον ὅτι ὁμοίως τῷ ἄλλῳ ἠθικῷ τόπῳ ἐγκατεσπάρησαν τοῖς ἀνθρώποις ἔννοιαι, ἀφ᾿ ὧν καὶ ὁ Ἡράκλειτος καὶ εἴ τις ἄλλος Ἑλλήνων ἢ βαρβάρων τοῦτ᾿ ἐνενόησε κατασκευάσαι. ἐκτίθεται γὰρ καὶ Πέρσας τοῦτο φρονοῦντας, παρατιθέμενος Ἡρόδοτον ἱστοροῦντα αὐτό. προσθήσομεν δὲ καὶ ἡμεῖς ὅτι καὶ Ζήνων ὁ Κιτιεὺς ἐν τῇ Πολιτείᾳ φησίν· „ἱερά τε οἰκοδομεῖν οὐδὲν δεήσει· ἱερὸν γὰρ οὐδὲν χρὴ νομίζειν οὐδὲ πολλοῦ ἄξιον καὶ ἅγιον, οἰκοδόμων τε ἔργον καὶ βαναύσων.“ σαφὲς οὖν ὅτι καὶ περὶ τούτου τοῦ δόγματος γέγραπται „ἐν ταῖς καρδίαις“ τῶν ἀνθρώπων γράμμασι θεοῦ τὸ πρακτέον.
pass_a_gloss: The things concerning idolatry, setting forth as their own from the word, and he establishes, saying they on this account do not consider them to be handmade gods, since it is not reasonable that the things made by the most wicked and evil-natured creators and often made by unjust men are gods. Therefore, wanting to make this common in the following, he sets forth the saying of Heraclitus, saying: 'Similarly, as if someone were to make a shelter for the houses, to do to those approaching as one would to lifeless things, as to gods.' Therefore, we must also speak about this, that similarly to the other ethical topic, notions have been sown among men, from which also Heraclitus and if any other Greek or barbarian has thought to establish this. For he also sets forth the Persians as thinking this, placing Herodotus as narrating it. We will also add that Zeno of Citium says in the Republic: 'There will be no need to build temples; for nothing should be considered holy or worthy of much and sacred, the work of builders and craftsmen.' It is clear, therefore, that also concerning this doctrine it has been written 'in the hearts' of men with the letters of God what is to be done.

choices.term: ποιεῖν τοὺς προσιόντας ὡς θεοῖς τοῖς ἀψύχοις

pass_b_english: The author treats the matter of idolatry as his own, drawing it from the word and building his case by stating that Christians do not consider handmade things to be gods on this account, since it is not reasonable for things made by the most wicked craftsmen and those of evil character, and often constructed by unjust men, to be gods. Wanting to make this point common ground in what follows, he cites the saying of Heraclitus: 'They act similarly to someone who would converse with houses, treating those who approach as if they were gods, though they are lifeless.' We must therefore say that, just as with the other ethical topic, notions have been sown among human beings, from which Heraclitus and any other Greek or barbarian who conceived of establishing this practice have drawn. For he also presents the Persians as holding this view, citing Herodotus as his witness. We will add that Zeno of Citium says in the Republic: 'There will be no need to build temples; for nothing should be considered holy or worth much and sacred, since it is the work of builders and craftsmen.' It is clear, therefore, that concerning this doctrine as well it has been written "in the hearts" of men with the letters of God what is to be done.

review.notes: Pass B introduces a significant mistranslation/hallucination of the Heraclitus quote that contradicts the Greek and Pass A. The Greek 'ὡς εἴ τις τοῖς δόμοις λεσχηνεύοιτο' (as if someone were to provide a shelter/banquet for the houses) is rendered in Pass B as 'as if they were to converse with houses', which changes the sense from providing/serving to conversing. Furthermore, Pass B adds 'though they are lifeless' at the end of the quote, whereas the Greek 'τοῖς ἀψύχοις' (the lifeless) is an adjective modifying the objects/gods being approached, not a separate clause about the houses.
reasons: Pass B mistranslates 'ὡς εἴ τις τοῖς δόμοις λεσχηνεύοιτο' as 'as if they were to converse with houses', whereas the Greek refers to providing a shelter or banquet (lescheneuo) for houses. Pass B also incorrectly structures the Heraclitus quote by adding 'though they are lifeless' as a separate thought, whereas the Greek 'τοῖς ἀψύχοις' modifies the objects of the action.

review.notes: The Greek text is correctly identified as 'Contra Celsum 1.5', and the English translation accurately reflects the content of the source. The title 'Idolatry' names the thought, not just a locus. All supplied source paragraphs (1) are checked and accounted for. No uncertainties are present. The translation preserves the original meaning, including the correct use of citations and the preservation of the author's arguments.
